subtype: Approach: divergent brainstorming of problems seen daily [Thinking]
passage: Friday, 11:40 pm. Got fed up tonight, so I made a Hostel Irritations list on the back of my drawing sheet: bags coming back from the wash after five days, watery dal, dead internet on Sundays, no printer after 9, the water heater. Too many. Instead of guessing, I went down the table at dinner and just asked people what annoys them most. Nikita from the second floor said the washing thing before I even finished my question. Tally by the end: washing 9 times, internet 4, dal 3, everything else once. So the washing delay is my candidate problem, not the dal, which is what I would have picked. Not a business yet. Just something worth studying properly. — Chaitanya

qa.q: How many times did the washing delay come up in the tally?
qa.a: The washing came up 9 times in the tally.

qa.q: What is Chaitanya feeling as the diary entry begins?
qa.a: Chaitanya is fed up, which is what pushes the list-making, but the mood turns curious by the end.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Chaitanya use to check this problem, and why?
qa.a: Chaitanya could interview a few residents about how they handle it today, because a tally shows what bothers people but not what they already do or pay.

qa.q: How does Nikita see the question?
qa.a: Nikita answers about the washing before the question is finished, which suggests it is a daily annoyance for Nikita and probably for others on the floor.

grounding: Shows divergent brainstorming of daily hostel annoyances, then choosing the one most often raised as a candidate problem.

subtype: Approach: talking to twenty potential users first [Action]
passage: Twenty done!! Spent nine evenings going room to room with my notebook. Every conversation started the same way: "How do you get your clothes washed right now, and what does it cost you?" I was sure the answer would be "we need an app". Nobody said it. Gurleen from B block said, "I don't care about tracking. I care that it is cheaper than the shop by the gate and I know the price before I hand over the bag." Fourteen of the twenty said something like that. Surprise charges make people angry. So the thing to sort out is pricing, not screens. Good thing I had not started coding yet. Tomorrow I write the numbers into one table. — Tarun

qa.q: How many of the twenty people said something like Gurleen?
qa.a: Fourteen of the twenty said something like that.

qa.q: What is Tarun feeling as the interviews finish?
qa.a: Tarun feels excited and relieved: the entry begins with 'Twenty done!!' and Tarun is glad to have found out before coding.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Tarun use next, and why?
qa.a: Tarun could test a simple price list with a few volunteers, because interviews say what people want and a trial shows whether they will act on it.

qa.q: How does Gurleen see the laundry problem?
qa.a: Gurleen wants a lower price than the shop by the gate and to know the cost beforehand, so an app matters less to Gurleen than a clear price.

grounding: Shows talking to about twenty potential users before building anything and learning that pricing matters more than a technical product.

subtype: Approach: minimum viable version with a manual service [Action]
passage:
"No app," said Avni, tapping the canteen table. "A group chat, a bag of clothes, and us."
"Us carrying bags? In front of everyone?" Ankita winced.
"Block C only, this Monday. We collect at seven, drop at the laundry, deliver on Thursday. Fifteen rupees a bag."
"And if nobody signs up?"
"Then we learn that before spending months on code."
"Fine. Poster?"
"Just a note on each door."
On Monday night the chat had nine names. On the next Thursday they carried the last bag up three floors. Ankita dropped it at a door and grinned. "Fourteen bags the first week. People actually paid." Avni was counting coins into a tin, barely listening. "Week two, then. We see if they come back."

qa.q: Which block did Avni and Ankita serve?
qa.a: They served Block C.

qa.q: What is Ankita feeling on first hearing the plan?
qa.a: Ankita feels embarrassed and unsure, wincing at the thought of carrying bags in front of everyone.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the founders try if the numbers stay small, and why?
qa.a: They could ask the paying customers what they liked and what nearly stopped them, because a small paying group can explain what a poster cannot.

qa.q: How might a student in Block C see this service?
qa.a: A student in Block C gets a note on the door, gives a bag at seven and gets it back on Thursday, so it looks like a simple, cheap favour with a clear price.

grounding: Shows running a hands-on pickup service through a chat app instead of coding, to test whether people will pay.

subtype: Approach: falling in love with the idea [Pitfall]
passage: Yamini, you asked what I would do differently, so let me be honest, from Ankita's side. I told everyone about my idea, a subscription box of snacks for students. Friends said, "Wow, so good!" A cousin said, "Hmm, maybe check the price?" and I nodded and moved on. I was in love. Within a month I had paid a designer for a logo, bought a domain, built a website with a tiny payment button. Then I asked people I did not know, at the bus stop, in the library. Not one wanted the box. Three said "cute". My savings were gone, and I had nothing to show but a nicely designed page. I should have asked strangers before anything else.

qa.q: What kind of business was Ankita's idea?
qa.a: It was a subscription box of snacks for students.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling in the early weeks after telling friends about the idea?
qa.a: Ankita was in love with the idea, excited and sure, which is why the cousin's polite doubt was brushed aside.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Ankita have used first, and why?
qa.a: Ankita could have asked strangers whether they would pay for a small trial box, because friends tend to be kind while strangers show real interest.

qa.q: How might the cousin have felt when the doubt was ignored?
qa.a: The cousin probably felt unheard, since the polite question about the price got only a nod.

grounding: Shows falling in love with an idea: hearing mostly praise, brushing aside doubts, spending savings on branding before testing demand with strangers.

passage:
Monday. In the library's quiet room, Irfan and Hafsa turned a sheet of paper over. "It is next November. We failed. Why?" Irfan wrote: exam weeks, one of us drifting away, customers who never come back. Hafsa added: no clear rule for who decides what. Beside each, they wrote a rule. Exam weeks: orders pause for five days, announced early. Drifting: a monthly honest check-in. No repeat buyers: ask every customer one question after the first order.
Thursday. Exam week arrived. They paused orders, posted a notice, and slept.
Three weeks later, the check-in surfaced that Hafsa was overloaded. They shifted two tasks. Irfan pinned the sheet above his desk.

qa.q: Which day did Irfan and Hafsa write their rules?
qa.a: They wrote their rules on Monday.

qa.q: What is Hafsa feeling at the three-week check-in?
qa.a: Hafsa feels overloaded and a bit stretched, which the check-in brings into the open so tasks can be shifted.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the founders add, and why?
qa.a: They could run a tiny paid trial with a few customers, because imagining failure lists risks while a trial shows which ones are real.

qa.q: How might a customer see the notice about paused orders?
qa.a: A customer would see a clear announcement that orders pause in exam week, which shows the team is reliable and protects the customer from surprise delays.

grounding: Shows a pre-mortem on a student venture, imagining failure a year ahead, naming likely causes and attaching a rule to each.

subtype: Approach: experiment and measure with a small pilot [Action]
passage:
Subject: Pilot results, honest version

Dear Mohit,

You suggested a pilot, so we ran one. Our target was 30 repeat orders in four weeks, counted only from customers who had ordered before. We logged each in one sheet, no rounding up. The final count is 22. We missed. At first it stung, but then we looked at the sheet: 17 of the 22 repeats came from Block B, where we delivered on the same evening every week. Other blocks got random days. So we are treating the miss as a clue, and next month we will fix delivery days everywhere and count again. May we send you the new sheet in four weeks?

Yash

qa.q: How many repeat orders did the team count?
qa.a: The final count is 22.

qa.q: What did Yash feel on seeing that the target was missed?
qa.a: At first it stung, so Yash felt disappointed, but then curious as the sheet pointed to a clue.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the team use if delivery days do not fix it, and why?
qa.a: They could phone a few one-time customers to ask why they did not reorder, because the numbers show what happened but not the reason.

qa.q: How might Mohit see this email?
qa.a: Mohit reads an honest count with the miss stated plainly and a next step, so Mohit can trust the team's numbers and help with the plan.

grounding: Shows a small pilot with a set target, an honest count, and treating a missed target as useful information.

subtype: Approach: analogy to an existing business model [Thinking]
passage: Tuesday night. Couldn't sleep, so I thought about the tiffin idea by comparing it with Kamla Mess near the old bus stand. Why does everyone stay loyal to it? I made a list. Trust: the same auntie cooks, nobody worries about hygiene, and the roti is never cold. Routine: the tiffin arrives at 1:15 exactly. Price: monthly, and missed meals are adjusted. Now the campus question. Trust can carry over if I show who cooks and how. Routine also carries, since class timings are fixed. The monthly price idea may work but students have irregular pocket money. Swati, my roommate, laughed: "So you're just copying Kamla Mess." Not copying. Borrowing the parts that fit. — Ganga

qa.q: What time does the tiffin arrive at Kamla Mess?
qa.a: The tiffin arrives at 1:15 exactly.

qa.q: What is Ganga feeling as the entry begins?
qa.a: Ganga is restless and curious, since sleep will not come and the mind keeps turning over why people stay loyal to the mess.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Ganga add to test the comparison, and why?
qa.a: Ganga could ask a few students what they would need to trust a new tiffin service, because the analogy comes from a town mess and a campus may work differently.

qa.q: How does Swati see Ganga's idea?
qa.a: Swati laughs and says Ganga is just copying Kamla Mess, which shows Swati sees the plan as a copy until Ganga explains it borrows only some parts.

grounding: Shows reasoning by analogy: comparing a campus tiffin idea with a successful local mess to decide which features would transfer.

subtype: Approach: rigid persistence despite weak signals [Pitfall]
passage: Sarita, since you keep saying you'll never quit your delivery idea, let old Dolma tell you mine. In my second year I began a small tea-and-snacks delivery in the hostel. After six months we had maybe ten customers. What did I do? I added things: a mobile app, then a loyalty card, then a fancy menu. My friend and cofounder Pema said, "Dolma, nobody is asking for these things." I said quitting would mean I had failed, and kept going. My attendance fell, my grades fell, and my savings went into features nobody used. Pema left in the eighth month. When I finally stopped, I felt lighter, not smaller. I wish I had listened at month six, when listening was cheap.

qa.q: How many customers did Dolma have after six months?
qa.a: Dolma had maybe ten customers after six months.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when Pema said nobody was asking for the new things?
qa.a: Dolma felt defensive and afraid of failing, treating quitting as proof of failure, so Dolma kept going.

qa.q: What choice at month six could Dolma have made instead, and why?
qa.a: Dolma could have asked customers why so few ordered, then changed the plan around the answers, because more features answered a question nobody had asked.

qa.q: How might Pema have felt watching Dolma add more and more features?
qa.a: Pema likely felt worried and unheard, having spoken plainly at month six and then leaving in the eighth month.

grounding: Shows rigid persistence: months of few customers, more features, no change of direction, and rising costs to grades and savings.

passage: In a dorm room in Warsaw, Emil and Wei opened the order log again. Their delivery service for student errands had been slow all autumn: a parcel here, a shopping run there. But tonight, sorting by date, Wei pointed. "Look at these bunches. December, January, June. Nearly everything is print jobs, and always the week before exams." Emil scrolled. "Lecture notes. People print them and hate queueing." They stopped the errands. For two days they wrote a plan: upload notes, choose a pickup time, collect from a locker outside the library. In the next exam period, orders tripled. Wei laughed at the counter. "We did not lose the idea. We just found the part people wanted."

qa.q: In which months did Wei notice bunches of print jobs?
qa.a: Wei noticed bunches of print jobs in December, January and June.

qa.q: What is Wei feeling when pointing at the bunches in the log?
qa.a: Wei feels a spark of excitement and discovery, pointing quickly as a pattern shows up in the data.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the founders use to check the new focus, and why?
qa.a: They could ask a few students what they would pay for printing and pickup, because the log shows what happened but not what students would keep using.

qa.q: How might a student with exams next week see the new service?
qa.a: A student uploads notes, picks a pickup time and collects them from a locker, so the student avoids the queue during a stressful week.

grounding: Shows adaptive replanning: noticing what customers actually used and narrowing the service to notes and printing, after which orders grew.

subtype: Approach: seeking a mentor and campus incubator advice [Action]
passage: Thursday, 10 pm. Today was our incubator slot. Steps: (1) Omkar and I cut our pitch to five slides. (2) We showed the mentor how the laundry service runs and what we charge. (3) The mentor asked how many paying customers we have. Eleven. They nodded and said that was a start, but before we talk to investors we need many more paying pilots. (4) They explained in plain words what registering a business involves and roughly what the costs are, and suggested we check details with a professional when the time comes. I wrote it all down. Not scary. My action list for tomorrow: find 20 more pilot customers. — Lalit

qa.q: How many paying customers did Lalit and Omkar have?
qa.a: They have eleven paying customers.

qa.q: What does Lalit feel about the mentor's advice?
qa.a: Lalit feels reassured and motivated, since the advice is not scary and comes with a clear action list.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the founders use alongside the mentor, and why?
qa.a: They could talk to a founder who has just started a similar service, because a mentor gives structure while a peer shows the daily reality.

qa.q: How might the mentor see the founders after this session?
qa.a: The mentor sees two founders with a real service and eleven paying customers who asked good questions, so the mentor points them to more paying pilots before any investors.

grounding: Shows seeking a mentor at a campus incubator, learning registration and cost basics, and hearing that paid pilots must come before investors.
